facts.label: Analysis by dimension
facts.text: Gross leverage has been stable near 2.9x while net leverage moved with cash. Net debt fell by USD 57.0 million in fiscal 2025 as operating cash flow of USD 198.4 million funded capital spending of USD 142.0 million and debt prepayments, then rose by USD 123.1 million in the nine months to 2026-09-30 as USD 129.5 million of capital spending, USD 102.8 million for Berry Aviation, USD 36.1 million of buybacks and USD 11.1 million of dividends exceeded operating cash flow of USD 94.0 million. The January 2026 refinancing replaced USD 400 million of 2028 secured notes with USD 500 million of 2033 secured notes, which lengthened the maturity profile and added about USD 100 million of principal, so creditors carry a larger gross debt base into the first full period with Berry Aviation and net leverage falls only if EBITDA grows or cash is rebuilt. Basis: calculation C7; calculation C18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5 and 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 112 and 96

facts.label: Analysis by dimension
facts.text: Data quality and definition risks are concentrated in EBITDA. The issuer states no EBITDA, so every leverage and cover figure rests on an analyst definition that includes gains on asset disposals and excludes power-by-hour amortization from the add-back; adding that amortization would lower LTM total leverage to 2.78x from 2.91x. The maturity ladder is the year-end 2025 pro forma schedule rather than a 2026-09-30 schedule, the principal of the two equipment financings is not stated, and the 2033 notes are dated January 2033 in the annual report but February 2033 in the quarterly reports. facts.label: Analysis by dimension
facts.text: The strongest contrary evidence to a rising-leverage concern is that net leverage is still below 2x, cover is above 5x, no maturity beyond amortisation falls before 2031 and the revolver is undrawn; that view wins if the Government Services segment returns to profit as the new UK and Irish contract transitions complete and Berry Aviation contributes a full year. It loses if the segment's operating loss persists, buybacks continue at the 2026 pace without free cash flow to fund them, or cash held outside the U.S. cannot be moved to the borrowers, which would be visible in the next quarter's net debt and the ABL availability statement. facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: - Government Services is the weak point: revenue grew 25.3% in the nine months of 2026 to USD 350.1 million, yet the segment swung to an operating loss of USD 2.6 million from income of USD 6.7 million. facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against caution is that Government Services work is on contracts of up to 10 years, the segment's loss is small against group operating income, offshore margins held at 17%, and the UK transition is scheduled to finish by the end of 2026, so the loss may prove a transition effect rather than a structural one. That view wins if segment operating income turns positive in the fourth quarter of 2026 and penalties fall as aircraft availability improves. It loses if the segment stays loss-making after the transitions end, if buybacks continue beyond free cash flow, or if the Norway sale is completed without proceeds applied to debt. Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 8 and 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32; calculation C14

It loses if the segment stays loss-making after the transitions end, if buybacks continue beyond free cash flow, or if the Norway sale is completed without proceeds applied to debt.

facts.text: Competitive rivalry is moderate because tenders are competitive and incumbents hold an advantage, supplier power is high because a few manufacturers supply aircraft and parts and parts delays already cost penalties, and buyer power is meaningful because large energy and government customers can cancel some contracts on notice, so margins are defended mainly by safety record and incumbency. facts.text: Over the next twelve to twenty-four months the supportive items are the scheduled end of the UK transition and a full year of Berry Aviation, and the headwinds are fuel prices linked to the conflict with Iran, supplier delays, labour negotiations and the cash cost of fleet renewal, so EBITDA growth is likely to be modest and free cash flow will depend on capital discipline. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The credit-relevant downside starts with the Government Services transition running past 2026, so penalties for aircraft availability and subcontractor costs persist while revenue grows more slowly than costs, which keeps the segment loss-making and holds group EBITDA flat. At the same time a weaker North Sea or lower utilisation in Europe would reduce offshore margins, and fuel price spikes would be recouped only with a lag, so operating cash flow would fall below capital spending and the buyback and dividend programme. Cash would then fall and the stated ABL availability would be the next source, which would raise net leverage and could shrink liquidity within a few quarters, but management has levers: the buyback authority can be suspended, capital spending can be deferred, and aircraft can be sold, so liquidity distress is unlikely without a combined loss of a large contract and a prolonged offshore downturn. The observable triggers are a continued segment operating loss after 2026, negative free cash flow after distributions, and falling stated availability. citations.quote: The credit-relevant downside starts with the Government Services transition running past 2026, so penalties for aircraft availability and subcontractor costs persist while revenue grows more slowly than costs, which keeps the segment loss-making and holds group EBITDA flat. At the same time a weaker North Sea or lower utilisation in Europe would reduce offshore margins, and fuel price spikes would be recouped only with a lag, so operating cash flow would fall below capital spending and the buyback and dividend programme. Cash would then fall and the stated ABL availability would be the next source, which would raise net leverage and could shrink liquidity within a few quarters, but management has levers: the buyback authority can be suspended, capital spending can be deferred, and aircraft can be sold, so liquidity distress is unlikely without a combined loss of a large contract and a prolonged offshore downturn. The observable triggers are a continued segment operating loss after 2026, negative free cash flow after distributions, and falling stated availability.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 14 and 30–32; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 8; calculation C6

facts.text: Overall, Bristow presents an adequate business profile supported by diversified long-dated contracts, moderate leverage and a lengthened maturity profile, but credit quality is constrained by thin free cash flow, a loss-making government segment and unverified creditor protections. Cash-flow durability appears adequate rather than strong because conversion fell, and refinancing capacity is likely to depend on offshore demand and on whether the Norway sale reduces debt. The primary downside path is a prolonged Government Services transition combined with continued shareholder returns. Further analysis would require the executed debt documents, issuer EBITDA definitions, a maturity schedule at the latest date and the proxy statement. Top risk: cash flow after capital spending and shareholder returns. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)

## Request

Source readiness for Bristow Group Inc. (issuer id vtol-1525221) as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is whether the five supplied filings can support the requested financial foundation, business and governance and fundamental credit work, and what remains missing.

## Findings
### Bottom line

The five supplied Bristow filings support the requested financial, business and fundamental credit work on the consolidated company, so creditor conclusions can rest on reported statements through the third quarter of 2026 but cannot cover covenant headroom, ratings or market pricing.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 1; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 93–96

Two annual reports and three quarterly reports give four discrete quarters, nine-month periods and a trailing twelve-month view from printed figures. The gaps that matter to creditors are the absence of any indenture or credit agreement, no printed maintenance covenant test, and an ABL availability figure that does not reconcile to commitments less letters of credit.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 52–53; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 13–14; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 33; calculation C4

## Request

## Findings
### Bottom line

Net leverage rose to 1.99x trailing twelve-month EBITDA at 2026-09-30 from 1.68x at the 2025 year-end while total leverage held near 2.91x, because 2026 cash went into an acquisition, capital returns and capital spending.
Basis: calculation C8; calculation C9; calculation C18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 5

Coverage is comfortable at 5.45x EBITDA to cash interest, and liquidity of USD 287.3 million sits against no scheduled maturity before 2031 beyond amortisation, but EBITDA is derived by the analyst because the issuer reports none, and covenant headroom is not established.
Basis: calculation C10; calculation C11; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 33; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 114

### Analysis by dimension

Gross leverage has been stable near 2.9x while net leverage moved with cash. Net debt fell by USD 57.0 million in fiscal 2025 as operating cash flow of USD 198.4 million funded capital spending of USD 142.0 million and debt prepayments, then rose by USD 123.1 million in the nine months to 2026-09-30 as USD 129.5 million of capital spending, USD 102.8 million for Berry Aviation, USD 36.1 million of buybacks and USD 11.1 million of dividends exceeded operating cash flow of USD 94.0 million. The January 2026 refinancing replaced USD 400 million of 2028 secured notes with USD 500 million of 2033 secured notes, which lengthened the maturity profile and added about USD 100 million of principal, so creditors carry a larger gross debt base into the first full period with Berry Aviation and net leverage falls only if EBITDA grows or cash is rebuilt.
Basis: calculation C7; calculation C18; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5 and 13; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 112 and 96

Cash interest cover of 5.45x for the twelve months to 2026-09-30 compares with 4.89x in fiscal 2025 because derived EBITDA rose while cash interest paid was almost unchanged. The cash measure flatters coverage relative to the income statement: interest expense, net rose by USD 8.5 million in the nine months because USD 6.5 million less interest was capitalised once aircraft entered service and because debt was higher during the refinancing, so an accrual-based cover would be lower than the cash-based cover shown.
Basis: calculation C10; calculation C6; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 3 and 33

Cash conversion weakened. Operating cash flow was 86.61% of derived EBITDA in fiscal 2025 and 66.98% for the twelve months to 2026-09-30 because nine months of 2026 absorbed USD 73.3 million of working capital, mainly receivables on higher activity and start-up costs on new government contracts paid before revenue starts. Free cash flow after capital spending fell from USD 56.4 million in fiscal 2025 to USD 12.3 million on a twelve-month basis and was negative in the nine months of 2026, when operating cash flow of USD 94.0 million was below capital expenditures of USD 129.5 million, so the 2026 buyback and dividend programme of USD 47.2 million was funded from cash on hand rather than from free cash flow.
Basis: calculation C15; calculation C22; calculation C23; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5 and 35

Liquidity of USD 287.3 million at 2026-09-30 is USD 59.6 million below the USD 346.9 million at 2025-12-31, of which USD 52.8 million is lower unrestricted cash and USD 6.8 million is lower stated ABL availability. Current maturities of long-term debt are USD 27.4 million and no other scheduled principal falls due before 2031, but about 75% of cash is held outside the U.S. against 43% three months earlier and repatriation could be taxed, so liquidity available to the U.S. borrowers is lower than the headline. The ABL Facility is undrawn, with USD 10.1 million of letters of credit outstanding, and its availability does not reconcile to commitments less letters of credit.

Basis: calculation C11; calculation C19; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4, 13–14 and 33; 10-Q_2026-06-30_vtol_vtol-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 31; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 72

Data quality and definition risks are concentrated in EBITDA. The issuer states no EBITDA, so every leverage and cover figure rests on an analyst definition that includes gains on asset disposals and excludes power-by-hour amortization from the add-back; adding that amortization would lower LTM total leverage to 2.78x from 2.91x. The maturity ladder is the year-end 2025 pro forma schedule rather than a 2026-09-30 schedule, the principal of the two equipment financings is not stated, and the 2033 notes are dated January 2033 in the annual report but February 2033 in the quarterly reports.
Basis: calculation C17; calculation C12; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 112 and 114; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 13

The strongest contrary evidence to a rising-leverage concern is that net leverage is still below 2x, cover is above 5x, no maturity beyond amortisation falls before 2031 and the revolver is undrawn; that view wins if the Government Services segment returns to profit as the new UK and Irish contract transitions complete and Berry Aviation contributes a full year. It loses if the segment's operating loss persists, buybacks continue at the 2026 pace without free cash flow to fund them, or cash held outside the U.S. cannot be moved to the borrowers, which would be visible in the next quarter's net debt and the ABL availability statement.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20, 28 and 36; calculation C9; calculation C15

## Gaps

- EBITDA is not stated by the issuer in any filing read, so EBITDA (Reported) is derived for every period; this restricts comparison with issuer or covenant leverage, leaves the EBITDA bridge not supplied because no add-backs are stated, and is a Medium gap, closed by an earnings release or compliance certificate that states EBITDA.

- Depreciation and amortization differs between the income statement and the cash flow statement by power-by-hour amortization, so EBITDA depends on which line is added back; this is a Medium gap, closed by the issuer's own EBITDA definition.

- Lines printed as a dash in the filings, namely the loss on extinguishment of debt, dividends, the acquisition and corporate segment revenue in the comparative periods, are Not supplied rather than zero; this restricts only those cells and is a Low gap.

- No balance sheet at 2025-09-30 is printed in the supplied filings, so that balance-sheet column holds only total equity from the statement of changes in equity; this restricts balance-sheet trends within 2025 and is a Low gap.
- Goodwill is not printed at the 2024 and 2025 year-ends because none existed on the balance sheet; the figure appears first at 2026-09-30 and is a Low gap for trend only.

- The principal and drawn amounts of the UKSAR Debt and the IRCG Debt are not stated, only carrying values and fees rounded to USD 0.1 million, so their contractual principal is not exactly established; this is a Medium gap, closed by the facility agreements or a principal table.

- The ABL margin level and any floor are not stated, only a 25 basis point margin reduction in the January 2026 amendment, so the ABL cost of funds is not established; this is a Low gap, closed by the ABL agreement.

- The legal rank of the ABL Facility, the UKSAR Debt and the IRCG Debt is not stated, so they are left out of the debt stack and the stack understates total debt; this is a Medium gap, closed by the facility and intercreditor documents.

- The ABL availability stated by the issuer does not equal commitments less letters of credit at 2026-03-31, 2026-09-30 or, on commitments then in force, 2025-12-31, and no borrowing base is described; liquidity uses the stated figure and this is a Medium gap, closed by the ABL agreement and a borrowing base certificate.

- No maturity schedule is printed at 2026-09-30, so the ladder is the pro forma schedule at 2025-12-31 and does not reflect 2026 amortisation payments; this is a Medium gap, closed by the next annual report schedule.
- The 2033 notes are dated January 2033 in the annual report and February 2033 in the quarterly reports; the quarterly wording is carried and this is a Low gap, closed by the indenture.

- The Berry Aviation price is USD 105.0 million in the second-quarter report and an estimated USD 110.9 million in the third-quarter report, and cash paid net of cash acquired exceeds consideration less cash acquired by USD 1.261 million; the cash flow line is used for net debt and this is a Low gap until purchase accounting is final.

- Quarterly columns are not built into the statement tables; the quarterly operating trend is shown separately from the reported comparison tables and quarterly cash flow is not derived, which is a Low gap for sequential cash flow analysis.

- Operating lease liabilities and the defined benefit pension plans are outside total debt by the method's definition; leases are shown separately and pension funded status is not quantified here, which is a Low definition gap for lease-adjusted leverage.

- Covenant levels and headroom are not established because no covenant test or governing document is supplied; this is a High gap for any covenant conclusion and is closed by the executed indenture and facility agreements.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Bristow is a publicly listed, contract-based aviation operator whose business mix is diversified enough to support its credit, but the Government Services transition is currently loss-making and 2026 capital returns and acquisitions are being funded from cash rather than from free cash flow.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 20, 30 and 36; calculation C11; calculation C9

Offshore Energy Services supplies 66% of revenue and Government Services 26%, with the three largest customers at 36% of revenue; the planned Norway sale and the Berry Aviation purchase shift the mix toward government work. No sponsor or controlling shareholder is identified in the filings supplied, so creditor risk is set by management's own policy, and the legal capacity for distributions is not established because no indenture is supplied.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 7 and 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 7 and 10; calculation C1; calculation C3
### Key findings

- Revenue is diversified by segment and geography but concentrated in a few customers and contracts. The largest customer, a government customer within Government Services, was 18.9% of revenue and the three largest were 36.4%, so a single contract transition or loss moves group earnings more than the segment mix suggests, and the ten largest customers were about 63% of revenue.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 12 and 135; calculation C3

- Government Services is the weak point: revenue grew 25.3% in the nine months of 2026 to USD 350.1 million, yet the segment swung to an operating loss of USD 2.6 million from income of USD 6.7 million. Transition costs on the UK and Irish search and rescue contracts, penalties of USD 9.8 million for aircraft availability tied to supply chain delays, and fuel costs above fuel revenue absorbed the new revenue, so margin recovery as the UK transition ends by December 31, 2026 is the main operating driver of deleveraging.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 8; calculation C11

- Offshore Energy Services carries group earnings: it earned operating income of USD 131.0 million at a 17% margin in the nine months, more than the group total after the segment and corporate losses. Management describes production-support work as less cyclical than exploration, but Europe revenue and flight hours fell in the period, which leaves the segment exposed to North Sea utilisation.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20 and 30–31; calculation C14

- Portfolio actions are reshaping the perimeter before their credit effect is visible. The Berry Aviation purchase at an estimated USD 110.9 million used USD 102.8 million of cash and added only 2.1% of nine-month revenue, while Norway generated 18.5% of fiscal 2025 revenue and the planned sale of its Norway Offshore Energy Services business has no stated terms, proceeds or timing.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 10 and 39; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 135; calculation C8; calculation C10

- Capital allocation turned shareholder-friendly in 2026 while free cash flow was thin. Dividends began in the first quarter and USD 47.2 million of dividends and buybacks were paid in nine months, with USD 96.0 million of the buyback authority left, so distributions are discretionary and funded from cash until operating cash flow recovers.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 17 and 36; calculation C6

- Governance disclosure supports monitoring but control rights are not established. The auditor issued an unqualified opinion and internal control was effective at the 2025 year-end, revenue from related parties, the Canadian affiliate and its co-owner, was only USD 22.9 million in nine months, and nationality rules require U.S. citizens to hold at least 75% of the parent's voting interests and local nationals to own and control the UK, Irish, Dutch and Norwegian operating companies, yet board composition, shareholder concentration and the covenant and restricted payment terms are not in the filings supplied.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 21–24, 84 and 92; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 12; calculation C7

- Labour contracts are a recurring cost and continuity risk: about 60% of employees are under collective agreements, the UK engineers' agreement expired in December 2025, and several Norwegian agreements were due to expire in March 2026, so wage settlements or disruption could hit the two largest offshore regions.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 19 and 35
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against caution is that Government Services work is on contracts of up to 10 years, the segment's loss is small against group operating income, offshore margins held at 17%, and the UK transition is scheduled to finish by the end of 2026, so the loss may prove a transition effect rather than a structural one. That view wins if segment operating income turns positive in the fourth quarter of 2026 and penalties fall as aircraft availability improves. It loses if the segment stays loss-making after the transitions end, if buybacks continue beyond free cash flow, or if the Norway sale is completed without proceeds applied to debt.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 8 and 12; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32; calculation C14
### Limitations

- The proxy statement is not supplied, so board independence, shareholder concentration and management ownership are not established, which limits the conclusion that no controlling shareholder or sponsor exists.

- No executed indenture or credit agreement is supplied, so the capacity for dividends, buybacks and further acquisitions is not established, which limits the conclusion that distributions are discretionary rather than constrained.
- Norway results are not printed for the quarters, so the earnings and perimeter effect of the planned sale is not quantified, which limits any view on the group's earnings after it.
- Berry Aviation is consolidated for under three months with preliminary purchase accounting, so its steady-state effect on Government Services margins is not established.
- Transition costs on the UK and Irish contracts are described but not quantified separately from base operating costs, so the pace of margin recovery cannot be dated precisely.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The one completed transaction is the acquisition of Berry Aviation, Inc., now Bristow Special Mission Inc., closed on 2026-07-13 for an estimated purchase price of USD 110.9 million, up from the USD 105.0 million announced in June 2026, subject to purchase price adjustments. It adds special mission, intelligence and surveillance, maintenance, unmanned systems and on-demand cargo operations, was paid in cash with USD 102.8 million of net cash outflow, contributed USD 26.3 million of revenue and USD 2.6 million of net income from the acquisition date, and recorded goodwill of USD 23.4 million, with acquisition costs of USD 7.4 million in nine months.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5 and 10–11; 10-Q_2026-06-30_vtol_vtol-20260630.htm.jsonl, page 18; calculation C8

The new debt issue in the period was the January 2026 offering of USD 500 million of senior secured notes due 2033, which are guaranteed by certain material domestic and foreign subsidiaries and secured by first-priority liens on substantially all assets of the issuer and guarantors, including certain pledged aircraft. Part of the proceeds redeemed the 2028 senior secured notes in full on 2026-03-01, and in January 2026 the ABL Facility was amended to cut commitments from USD 85 million to USD 70 million and extend maturity to 2031. The company also announced plans on 2026-06-23 to pursue the sale of its Norway Offshore Energy Services business, which was not classified as held for sale or as discontinued operations because not all criteria had been met, and sold two AW189 heavy helicopters in sale and leaseback transactions in the nine months.
Basis: 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 7, 13 and 33; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 112 and 114

spans.text: # CP-2 Fundamental credit: Bristow Group Inc.
## Request

Fundamental credit synthesis for Bristow Group Inc. (issuer id vtol-1525221) as of 2026-11-18, on the credit snapshot pathway. The scope is the overall credit view, strengths and weaknesses, downside path, materiality ranking and monitoring triggers drawn from the five supplied filings and the earlier module outputs.

## Findings
### Bottom line

Bristow's fundamental credit profile is adequate, with net leverage of 1.99x, interest cover of 5.45x and no large maturity before 2031, but its cash cushion is thinning because free cash flow is small, shareholder returns have started and Government Services is loss-making.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C1; calculation C4

Creditors are supported by a long-dated secured capital structure and liquidity of USD 287.3 million, but the earnings measures are the analyst's because the issuer reports no EBITDA, and covenant headroom and legal capacity are not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 33; calculation C4
### Key findings

- Leverage is moderate but has turned up. Net debt was 1.99x trailing twelve-month EBITDA at 2026-09-30 against 1.68x at the 2025 year-end, while total debt stayed near 2.91x, because 2026 cash paid for an acquisition, capital spending and shareholder returns, so deleveraging now depends on EBITDA growth rather than on repayment.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C1; calculation C2; calculation C6

- Coverage, liquidity and maturities are adequate. EBITDA covered cash interest 5.45x, liquidity of USD 287.3 million is about 10.50x current maturities of USD 27.4 million, and the schedule shows only amortisation before 2031, so a refinancing event is distant and the main near-term risk is operating cash flow, not market access.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 114; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 4 and 33; calculation C4

- Cash flow is the weak link. Free cash flow was only USD 12.3 million on a twelve-month basis against USD 56.4 million in fiscal 2025, operating cash flow converted 66.98% of EBITDA, and USD 47.2 million of dividends and buybacks were paid in nine months while free cash flow was negative, so distributions are being funded from the cash balance.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation C5; calculation C6

- Business risk is moderate and concentrated in one transition. Offshore Energy Services earns the group profit and Government Services holds ten-year contracts, but the government segment made an operating loss of USD 2.6 million in nine months and the three largest customers are 36% of revenue, so a slow end to the UK and Irish transitions would hit group earnings directly.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 20 and 30; calculation C7

- Earnings quality limits comparability. The issuer reports no EBITDA, derived EBITDA includes disposal gains of about 2.98% of the total, and adding power-by-hour amortization would lower total leverage to 2.78x, while excluding disposal gains would raise it to 3.00x, so the range of reasonable leverage is wider than one point estimate suggests.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C8; calculation C9

- Financial policy and governance are mixed rather than adverse. There is no sponsor or controlling holder in the filings and audit and reporting are sound, but dividends and buybacks began in 2026 and the restricted payment terms that would constrain them are not supplied, so the discipline of future distributions is not established.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 52–53
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence for a better view is that derived EBITDA grew faster than debt, the secured notes extended maturity to 2033, the ABL Facility is undrawn and the offshore business holds a steady margin, so the nine-month cash drain may be a one-off from the acquisition and transition costs. The strongest evidence for a weaker view is that free cash flow is close to zero before capital returns and the new government contracts are still loss-making. The view improves if Government Services turns profitable after the UK transition ends and buybacks stay within free cash flow, and weakens if free cash flow stays near USD 12.3 million while distributions continue.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 8; calculation C3; calculation C5
### Limitations

- Leverage and cover use the analyst's derived EBITDA, so the view that leverage is moderate could shift, for total debt, from 2.78x to 3.00x with the treatment of power-by-hour amortization and disposal gains.

- The maturity schedule is printed only at the 2025 year-end on a pro forma basis, so the statement that no maturity falls before 2031 beyond amortisation rests on that schedule and the later narrative rather than on a 2026 schedule.
- Stated ABL availability is USD 6.0 million below commitments less letters of credit and the reason is not described, so the liquidity conclusion carries that unexplained difference.
- No forward model, guidance or peer and market data are supplied, so the outlook and the downside path are qualitative and the profile is not benchmarked against comparable issuers.
- Covenant headroom is not established, so the view says nothing about default triggers or the point at which creditors would gain control rights.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strength: a diversified, long-dated contract base. Offshore Energy Services, Government Services and Other Services contributed 66%, 26% and 8% of fiscal 2025 revenue, government search and rescue contracts run for ten years, and the three largest customers were 36% of revenue, so earnings do not hang on one market and revenue visibility is better than for a spot-priced operator, which lowers the chance that a single market shock threatens debt service.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 7–8 and 12; calculation C7

Strength: moderate leverage and strong coverage. Total debt was 2.91x and net debt 1.99x derived EBITDA with cash interest covered 5.45x, so a material fall in earnings could be absorbed before coverage reaches a level that stresses interest payments, which supports the view that the capital structure is serviceable at current earnings.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C1

Strength: a lengthened and secured maturity profile with undrawn liquidity. The 2033 secured notes replaced the 2028 notes, the schedule shows only amortisation before 2031, and the ABL Facility is undrawn with letters of credit outstanding, so refinancing risk before 2031 is limited and the revolver provides a backstop.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 114; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 13–14; calculation C4

Strength: audited reporting and no identified sponsor. The auditor gave an unqualified opinion with effective internal control and no sponsor or controlling holder is named, so monitoring is possible from filings and no sponsor extraction behaviour is documented.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 92

Weakness: thin free cash flow against rising claims on cash. Free cash flow was USD 12.3 million on a twelve-month basis while dividends and buybacks of USD 47.2 million, an acquisition and unfunded aircraft commitments drew on cash, so liquidity has fallen and net leverage rose, which leaves less cushion if earnings weaken.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation C5; calculation C6

Weakness: the Government Services transition. The segment's operating loss, availability penalties and fuel costs above fuel revenue absorbed new revenue in nine months, so earnings growth depends on the UK transition ending on schedule and costs receding, and delay would hold group EBITDA below what the contract base implies.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 30–32; calculation C7

Weakness: customer concentration and labour exposure. The largest customer is a government customer within Government Services, about 60% of employees are under collective agreements and the UK engineers' agreement has expired, so a contract loss or a labour dispute in the UK or Norway would hit a large share of earnings.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 19 and 35

Weakness: unverified legal and covenant protections. No indenture or credit agreement is supplied and distributions are discretionary, so creditors cannot confirm what limits dividends, buybacks and further secured or other debt, which weakens confidence in the creditor protection behind the structure.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 52–53

### Operating model, margin and cash conversion

Offshore Energy Services supplies most revenue and more than the group's total operating profit, because production-support contracts for offshore platforms carry fixed monthly fees plus flight-hour payments, while Government Services adds ten-year search and rescue contracts whose start-up costs have so far held margins below break-even. Cost flexibility is limited because personnel and maintenance are the largest cost lines and about 60% of employees are under collective agreements, so margin falls quickly when utilisation drops, and the fleet needs continued capital spending that absorbed most operating cash flow over the last twelve months.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 19–20; calculation C5
### Credit-translated frameworks

Competitive rivalry is moderate because tenders are competitive and incumbents hold an advantage, supplier power is high because a few manufacturers supply aircraft and parts and parts delays already cost penalties, and buyer power is meaningful because large energy and government customers can cancel some contracts on notice, so margins are defended mainly by safety record and incumbency. Regulation matters more than macro factors: nationality ownership rules limit foreign control, and fuel price swings are recouped with a lag, which makes fuel a margin timing risk rather than a solvency risk. Credit-translated strengths are contract tenor, diversification and a lengthened maturity profile; weaknesses are thin free cash flow, the government transition and customer concentration; opportunities are the end of the transitions and Berry Aviation; threats are labour disputes, supplier delays and a Norway sale without debt reduction.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 13 and 33; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, page 40
### Outlook

Over the next twelve to twenty-four months the supportive items are the scheduled end of the UK transition and a full year of Berry Aviation, and the headwinds are fuel prices linked to the conflict with Iran, supplier delays, labour negotiations and the cash cost of fleet renewal, so EBITDA growth is likely to be modest and free cash flow will depend on capital discipline. Over three to five years the 2031 and 2033 maturities are the key events and the 2036 UKSAR Debt amortises, so the capital structure should be refinanceable if leverage stays near current levels, but that depends on contract renewals and offshore energy demand that the filings do not forecast.
Basis: 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, pages 8 and 114; 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 23 and 40
### Downside scenario

The credit-relevant downside starts with the Government Services transition running past 2026, so penalties for aircraft availability and subcontractor costs persist while revenue grows more slowly than costs, which keeps the segment loss-making and holds group EBITDA flat. At the same time a weaker North Sea or lower utilisation in Europe would reduce offshore margins, and fuel price spikes would be recouped only with a lag, so operating cash flow would fall below capital spending and the buyback and dividend programme. Cash would then fall and the stated ABL availability would be the next source, which would raise net leverage and could shrink liquidity within a few quarters, but management has levers: the buyback authority can be suspended, capital spending can be deferred, and aircraft can be sold, so liquidity distress is unlikely without a combined loss of a large contract and a prolonged offshore downturn. The observable triggers are a continued segment operating loss after 2026, negative free cash flow after distributions, and falling stated availability.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-Q_2026-09-30_vtol_vtol-20260930.htm.jsonl, pages 5, 14 and 30–32; 10-K_2025-12-31_vtol_vtol-20251231.htm.jsonl, page 8; calculation C6
### Overall credit view

Overall, Bristow presents an adequate business profile supported by diversified long-dated contracts, moderate leverage and a lengthened maturity profile, but credit quality is constrained by thin free cash flow, a loss-making government segment and unverified creditor protections. Cash-flow durability appears adequate rather than strong because conversion fell, and refinancing capacity is likely to depend on offshore demand and on whether the Norway sale reduces debt. The primary downside path is a prolonged Government Services transition combined with continued shareholder returns. Further analysis would require the executed debt documents, issuer EBITDA definitions, a maturity schedule at the latest date and the proxy statement. Top risk: cash flow after capital spending and shareholder returns.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)
